nameStory: The long-billed dowitcher gets its name from its impressively lengthy bill, which is noticeably longer than its close cousin, the short-billed dowitcher. The word 'dowitcher' itself comes from the Iroquois language and was first recorded by European settlers in 1841. These two species were actually thought to be the same bird until 1950, when scientists finally recognized they were separate species!
description: The long-billed dowitcher is a chunky, medium-sized shorebird that looks like it's wearing rust-colored pajamas during breeding season. Its most striking feature is its extraordinarily long, straight bill that it uses like a sewing machine to probe deep into mud for food. In breeding plumage, it sports a beautiful rufous (reddish-brown) head and belly, with a mottled darker back that provides excellent camouflage. When it takes flight, you'll catch a flash of bright white on its rump that's unmistakable.

idTips.label: Flight Call
idTips.description: Listen for a sharp, high-pitched 'keek' call that sounds thinner and more piercing than its short-billed cousin's deeper 'tu-tu-tu' notes

idTips.label: Feeding Behavior
idTips.description: Watch for the distinctive 'sewing machine' motion as it rapidly probes its bill up and down in the mud, often with its entire bill and head underwater

idTips.label: Bill Shape
idTips.description: The bill feels sturdy if handled and appears notably long and straight, like a knitting needle, often appearing longer than the bird's head

idTips.label: White Rump Patch
idTips.description: In flight, look for a bright white triangular patch on the lower back that flashes conspicuously against the darker wings and back

idTips.label: Breeding Plumage
idTips.description: Rich rust-orange coloring covers the head, neck, and belly, giving the bird a warm, cinnamon-toast appearance from late spring through summer

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Almost always found in freshwater environments - muddy pond edges, marsh borders, and flooded fields rather than ocean beaches

habitat: In New England, look for long-billed dowitchers along the muddy edges of freshwater ponds, marshes, and flooded agricultural fields. They prefer shallow areas where they can wade and probe deeply into soft, organic-rich mud for invertebrates. Unlike many shorebirds, they rarely venture onto saltwater beaches, sticking to inland wetlands and occasionally sewage treatment ponds.

seasonality.spring: Migration peaks in late April through May, when birds show their brightest rufous breeding plumage and are most vocal with their distinctive calls.
seasonality.summer: Rare in New England during summer as most birds continue north to Arctic breeding grounds, though occasional non-breeding individuals may linger.
seasonality.fall: Most common from August through October during southward migration, often in dull brownish-gray winter plumage that makes identification challenging.
seasonality.winter: Uncommon in New England winters, with most birds continuing south, though a few may overwinter in unfrozen wetlands during mild years.

funFact: Long-billed dowitchers can actually taste their food underwater! They have sensitive nerve endings at the tip of their bills that let them identify and capture worms and other prey in murky water without ever seeing what they're eating - like having taste buds on your fingertips.
confusionNotes: The biggest identification challenge is telling it apart from the short-billed dowitcher, especially in winter when both species look nearly identical in drab gray-brown plumage. Remember this trick: long-billed dowitchers say 'keek' (a thin, sharp note) while short-billed dowitchers say 'tu-tu-tu' (deeper, more musical). When in doubt, listen - their voices are the most reliable way to tell them apart.
contextualKnowledge: These two dowitcher species were considered the same bird for over a century because they look so similar, leading to decades of confused birdwatchers and muddled field records. Even today, many birders throw up their hands and simply record 'dowitcher species' when they can't get a good look or hear the call clearly.
compareHints: Compared to the short-billed dowitcher, the long-billed has a noticeably longer, thinner bill and prefers freshwater habitats over salt marshes. The long-billed also tends to probe deeper and more rapidly when feeding, often submerging its entire head. Most reliably, their calls are completely different - long-billed gives sharp 'keek' notes while short-billed produces mellower 'tu-tu-tu' calls.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its only close relative, the long-billed dowitcher, the short-billed species typically shows more barring on the flanks during breeding season and has a slightly less bulbous bill tip.
